Computation

Kyungsub Lee

2026-10-16

Source: vignettes/articles/computation.Rmd
computation.Rmd

This guide covers calculation choices for the built-in likelihood. Start with Get started. For model interpretation and standard errors, see Fitting and inference.

Working example 

library(emhawkes)

h <- new("hspec",
  mu = c(0.2, 0.2),
  alpha = matrix(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.9, 0.5), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  beta = matrix(2.25, 2, 2)
)
set.seed(1107)
path <- hsim(h, size = 1000)
fit <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type)
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
summary(fit)
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 33 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -970.1408 
#> 4  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value  Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.19095    0.01638  11.656  < 2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.48217    0.07430   6.489 8.64e-11 ***
#> alpha1.2  0.98625    0.09576  10.300  < 2e-16 ***
#> beta1.1   2.07987    0.17203  12.091  < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

Likelihood engines

With automatic engine selection, numeric Hawkes specifications use a compiled Rcpp engine for likelihood evaluation and inference, including multi-kernel models, unequal decay rates, and numeric mark effects. Standalone likelihood and inference also support parameter-only component functions returning plain numeric matrices. Observed baselines and observed or sequential state-dependent impacts also use C++. Baselines cannot depend on latent intensities. Unsupported function signatures use R. Mark densities, residual-distribution models, and numeric inputs with custom classes use R. The fitting adapters below also select C++ automatically for supported callback models.

The emhawkes.engine option controls the built-in likelihood:

Setting Role
"auto" (default) Use C++ for supported models and R otherwise. Supported fitting adapters receive this acceleration automatically.
"r" Force the R likelihood for comparison or troubleshooting.
"cpp" Require C++ support; report an error for unsupported models.

Simulation selects its path separately. hsim() uses an Rcpp event loop for plain numeric mu, alpha, and beta and strictly positive baselines. Functions with exactly one param argument can also use this loop after the existing setup resolves them to plain numeric values. Multivariate and mapped multi-kernel models support both equal and unequal within-row decay rates. Unequal rates retain the R thinning algorithm, including rejected random draws. The likelihood engine option does not force either simulation path.

With equal rates within each row, simulation also supports numeric eta, mark generators requesting no event context, and impacts requesting only lambda_component_n (or no context). Optional parameter defaults stay in the original R functions; these functions must return real numeric marks or components. The event loop runs in C++, calls the user functions in R, and synchronizes RNG state around each call, including errors and nested simulations. Each impact receives a fresh component snapshot with its original attributes. Models requiring other event context, ..., event-dependent baselines, custom residual distributions, zero baselines, or unequal rates with callbacks continue to use R. The existing numeric loop remains a separate compiled path.

Both simulation paths preserve the R random-draw order: all baseline exponential candidates are generated before all excitation uniforms. size includes the initial row; a one-row numeric simulation consumes no randomness. Simulation callbacks retain their requested arguments, and ... retains the full supported context. Request only the state you need to reduce history copying on long R paths.

Setting "cpp" is unnecessary to accelerate models already supported by "auto". Inspect fit_diagnostics(fit)$computation$engine for the engines actually used and any automatic fallback reason. Engine selection does not enable analytic gradients: request gradient = "analytic" explicitly; unsupported analytic gradients produce an error. A custom mylogLik bypasses built-in engine selection. Installing from source requires a C++ compiler and Rcpp; Windows source installations require Rtools.

hspec2 <- h
inter_arrival2 <- path$inter_arrival
type2 <- path$type

The following example compares standalone numeric likelihood calculations.

This function restores the previous option after each call.

engine_loglik <- function(engine) {
  previous <- options(emhawkes.engine = engine)
  on.exit(options(previous))
  as.numeric(logLik(hspec2, inter_arrival = inter_arrival2, type = type2))
}
c(R = engine_loglik("r"), automatic = engine_loglik("auto"))
#>         R automatic 
#> -974.2809 -974.2809

Recorded calculation methods

The fit also records its calculation methods:

calculation <- fit_diagnostics(fit)$computation
calculation$engine   # Requested engine, actual engines and auto fallback reason.
#> $requested
#> [1] "auto"
#> 
#> $used
#> [1] "cpp"
#> 
#> $fallback_reason
#> NULL
calculation$gradient # Numeric, analytic or user-supplied score.
#> $requested
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $used
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $reason
#> NULL
calculation$hessian # Requested and applied final-Hessian methods.
#> $requested
#> [1] "maxLik"
#> 
#> $finalHessian
#> NULL
#> 
#> $used
#> [1] "maxLik_numeric"
#> 
#> $reason
#> NULL
#> 
#> $maxLik_skipped
#> [1] FALSE

An auto fit can record both "cpp" and "r" if it switches during estimation. The record includes final curvature evaluations and survives saveRDS(). Older fits without this record return recorded = FALSE and NA for unrecorded methods. The existing curvature checks remain available at the top level.

With final_hessian = "stable", computation$hessian$used is "scaled_score_Richardson" when the built-in analytic score is available, or "scaled_central_Richardson" for likelihood differences. The optimizer can still use the default numerical gradient. Supply the same component jacobian list as for analytic optimization to enable score-based curvature for function models. fit_diagnostics(fit)$score_fallback_reason explains a failed score attempt. The explicit r engine uses likelihood differences.

For unconstrained BFGS, CG, Nelder-Mead, and SANN fits, stable curvature skips maxLik’s separate final Hessian when neither hess nor finalHessian is supplied. computation$hessian$maxLik_skipped records this choice. The stable checks and standard errors are unchanged; original_hessian is NULL when the extra pass is omitted. Set finalHessian = TRUE to retain that pass. Newton methods, constrained fits, and the default final_hessian = "maxLik" retain their handling.

Analytic gradients

hfit() uses this engine for its built-in likelihood. Numerical differentiation remains the default. For numeric Hawkes models, request the Rcpp analytic gradient:

fit <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type, gradient = "analytic")
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.

This option supports shared and fixed parameters, multi-kernel mappings, numeric mark effects, and derivatives of automatic initial states. It computes the likelihood and score with native recursions. Observed baselines and current-state impacts require the Jacobians described below. Full intensity histories, custom likelihoods, mark densities, residual distributions, equality constraints, and BHHH are not yet supported. Singular automatic initialization requires explicit lambda_component0. A supplied grad takes precedence. A supplied hess is retained; otherwise maxLik can differentiate the analytic gradient for curvature. The optimizer’s path and last digits may differ from numerical differentiation. The gradient report describes accuracy, full-fit timings, and the state-dependent extension.

Component functions and Jacobians

Parameter-only mu, alpha, beta, and eta functions can also use the analytic option when supplied with their exact Jacobians. For example, this function fixes one excitation entry at zero:

alpha_fun <- function(param = c(a = 0.2, b = 0.1)) {
  matrix(c(param["a"], 0, param["b"], param["a"]), 2)
}
alpha_jac <- cbind(a = c(1, 0, 0, 1), b = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
h_fun <- new("hspec", mu = h@mu, alpha = alpha_fun, beta = h@beta)
fit_fun <- hfit(h_fun, path$inter_arrival, path$type,
  gradient = "analytic", jacobian = list(alpha = alpha_jac))
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.

Jacobian rows follow as.vector() of the returned matrix; columns are named with its param names. For nonlinear transformations, supply a function(param) that returns the Jacobian at that parameter vector. Components and Jacobians must be deterministic functions of param with fixed matrix dimensions. The package does not derive or verify the formulas automatically. A component with param = numeric(0) needs no Jacobian. Shared parameter names receive the sum of all component contributions. Missing or malformed Jacobians produce an error. The analytic fit evaluates component functions in R and the likelihood and scores in Rcpp. With the default "auto" engine, supported function-valued models also use C++ with numerical differentiation, without Jacobians:

fit_numeric <- hfit(h_fun, path$inter_arrival, path$type)
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.

The functions must return plain numeric matrices of constant dimensions and be deterministic in param. Observed-state impact functions also use this numerical path without Jacobians, including count- and mark-dependent impacts and the Hawkes flocking example. Numerical C++ fitting also supports observed baselines and sequential impacts that explicitly request current or historical intensity states, including the bid-ask example. Mark densities and residual distributions remain unsupported. Supplied grad and hess are retained. Automatic selection uses R for unsupported specifications; forcing "cpp" reports unsupported features. Callback errors propagate. Callbacks must be deterministic with fixed captures; detecting an unsupported state read through ... can require a retry in R. Standalone logLik() and infer = TRUE also use C++ for parameter-only component functions, observed baselines, and observed or sequential state-dependent impacts. The default automatic selection therefore accelerates replay of restored models with these components. Each callback keeps its own defaults; standalone replay does not apply parameter-sharing rules from fitting.

Observed impacts and baselines

Observed-state impact functions can use the analytic option with jacobian = list(impact = impact_jac). They may depend on observed N, Nc, marks, types, and times, and on the resolved mu, alpha, and beta matrices. Counts at row n include that event. The event’s impact affects subsequent intensities in the kernel columns selected by its type.

For jacobian$impact, param is the full named optimization vector. Return a matrix with one row per impact entry in column-major order and one named column per fitted parameter, including zero columns. Include derivatives through any core matrices used by the impact. The impact function keeps receiving its local parameters. See ?hfit for an example and the callback contract. Current-component feedback can use the analytic option with additional derivatives below. Default numerical fitting uses C++ for supported callbacks. Declare lambda_component_n to receive the current pre-jump component matrix. Declare lambda or lambda_component only when full pre-jump histories are needed. Observed baselines may use counts and marks, return a dimensions-by-one matrix, and remain constant between events. They cannot depend on latent intensities. See the bid-ask benchmark for the state convention, compatibility checks and timings.

For an observed baseline, analytic fitting requires jacobian$mu with one row per event dimension and one named column per full fitted parameter, including zero columns. Its callback receives observations and the full named param. Include dependencies through resolved core components. The baseline itself continues to receive its local parameters.

Current-state Jacobians

An impact that declares lambda_component_n can use:

fit <- hfit(h, inter_arrival, type, mark, lambda_component0 = initial,
  gradient = "analytic", jacobian = list(mu = mu_jac, alpha = alpha_jac,
    impact = list(param = impact_param_jac, state = impact_state_jac)))

Here impact$param differentiates the impact with respect to all fitted parameters holding the current state fixed. It includes direct dependencies through core components. impact$state differentiates impact entries with respect to current component entries. Both state axes follow as.vector() column-major order; the matrix is components-by-components. The package propagates derivatives through decay, selected jumps, and automatic initialization. Arbitrary reads of full lambda or lambda_component histories remain unsupported for analytic fitting. All callbacks must be deterministic, and supplied derivatives must exist at evaluated parameters. The Bid-ask analytic-gradient section contains the complete Jacobians and fit. See the state-gradient report for accuracy checks and timings. Numerical differentiation remains the default.

Time and memory

When only the current state is needed, use lambda_component_n. Full histories need storage proportional to events times dimensions times kernels. If a callback retains these histories, snapshot-preserving copies can make cumulative copying grow quadratically with event count. Peak live memory and cumulative allocation are different costs. See the scaling measurements for time, allocation and memory comparisons.

See the count, mark and flocking benchmark for complete-fit timings and accuracy checks.

Observed-baseline derivatives retain the event-row derivative and the row sum needed by the integral, together with the initial Jacobian. This reduces storage from order events * dimensions * parameters to events * parameters when the compact array payload is smaller. Supply a matrix when the total Jacobian is constant; it then needs no event path. Small dimensions retain the dense path. Callback order and the public jacobian$mu interface are unchanged. State-Jacobian callback allocations remain separate. See the storage study.

Bid-ask analytic gradient

First run the Bid-ask price model. The code below continues in that R session, using h_ba, hr_ba, mle_ba, initial_ask_price, initial_bid_price, initial_level, and initial_mid_price.

The current-component version also supports an optional analytic gradient. The baseline Jacobian uses all fitted parameter names; the parameter-only alpha Jacobian uses its local names. For impact, supply separate derivatives with respect to parameters (holding the current state fixed) and the current state. All matrix entries use as.vector() column-major order. In particular, the state Jacobian differentiates the pre-jump row sums subtracted by impact. Counts and mark totals are observed data and have zero parameter derivative. The baseline uses counts before the event, while impact uses counts after it.

# Exact derivatives for the current-component Bid-ask example.
bid_ask_jacobians <- function(initial_ask_price, initial_bid_price, initial_level,
    initial_mid_price = (initial_ask_price + initial_bid_price) / 2) {
  force(initial_ask_price); force(initial_bid_price); force(initial_level); force(initial_mid_price)
  market_state <- function(n, Nc, after = FALSE) {
    if (n == 1L) return(list(level = initial_level, mid = initial_mid_price))
    k <- if (after) n else n - 1L
    ask <- initial_ask_price + Nc[k, 1] - Nc[k, 2]
    bid <- initial_bid_price + Nc[k, 3] - Nc[k, 4]
    list(level = initial_level + Nc[k, 1] - Nc[k, 2] - (Nc[k, 3] - Nc[k, 4]),
      mid = (ask + bid) / 2)
  }
  mu_jac <- function(param, n, Nc, ...) {
    s <- market_state(n, Nc)
    J <- matrix(0, 4, length(param), dimnames = list(NULL, names(param)))
    J[c(1, 4), 'mu1'] <- 1
    if (s$level > 0) J[c(2, 3), 'zeta1'] <- s$level / s$mid
    J
  }
  alpha_jac <- matrix(0, 16, 5, dimnames = list(NULL,
    c('alpha_s1', 'alpha_m', 'alpha_s2', 'alpha_w1', 'alpha_w2')))
  alpha_jac[c(1, 16), 'alpha_s1'] <- 1
  alpha_jac[c(5, 12), 'alpha_m'] <- 1
  alpha_jac[c(9, 8), 'alpha_s2'] <- 1
  alpha_jac[c(2, 15), 'alpha_w1'] <- 1
  alpha_jac[c(3, 14), 'alpha_w2'] <- 1
  impact_param_jac <- function(param, n, Nc, ...) {
    s <- market_state(n, Nc, after = TRUE)
    J <- matrix(0, 16, length(param), dimnames = list(NULL, names(param)))
    J[c(6, 7, 10, 11), 'xi'] <- s$level / s$mid
    J
  }
  impact_state_jac <- matrix(0, 16, 16)
  impact_state_jac[c(6, 10), c(2, 6, 10, 14)] <- -1
  impact_state_jac[c(7, 11), c(3, 7, 11, 15)] <- -1
  list(mu = mu_jac, alpha = alpha_jac,
    impact = list(param = impact_param_jac, state = impact_state_jac))
}

ba_jac <- bid_ask_jacobians(initial_ask_price, initial_bid_price, initial_level,
  initial_mid_price)
mle_ba_analytic <- hfit(h_ba, inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival,
  type = hr_ba$type, mark = hr_ba$mark,
  lambda_component0 = matrix(1, 4, 4), gradient = "analytic",
  jacobian = ba_jac, final_hessian = "stable")
stopifnot(abs(mle_ba_analytic$maximum - mle_ba$maximum) < 2e-6)
cbind(numeric = coef(mle_ba), analytic = coef(mle_ba_analytic))
fit_diagnostics(mle_ba_analytic)$computation

Numerical differentiation remains the default. The optimization path and last digits may differ. Analytic fitting does not support arbitrary reads of the full lambda or lambda_component histories. Branches in this example depend only on observations. Parameter-dependent branch thresholds need separate differentiability checks. Faster gradients do not resolve weak identification or guarantee reliable standard errors.
